newsitem.title: singapore: Singapore economy on track for recovery - economists.
newsitem.headline: Singapore economy on track for recovery - economists.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil exports fell by a smaller-than-expected 2.1 percent in March, indicating the economy was on track for recovery in the second half of the year, economists said on Monday.
The Trade Development Board said exports of non-oil goods fell a nominal 2.1 percent year-on-year in March to S$7.67 billion (US$5.33 billion) after falling 7.9 percent in February.
Market forecasts had generally been more pessimistic. A Reuters poll of 11 economists last week had predicted a 4.5 percent drop.
"The figure...means the recovery story is reasonably intact and we should see it in the second half," said Rajeev Malik, senior economist with Jardine Fleming International Securities.
Liew Yin Sze, chief economist with J.M. Sassoon, agreed.
"The March figures have allayed some fears about whether there would be a recovery for the Singapore economy in the second half," he told Reuters.
He said while the latest figures showed continued weakness in some sectors, they also indicated the worst was probably over and the trend should improve in coming months.

Liew said the March figures also helped counter the view that recent news of manufacturers, like disk-drive maker Seagate, relocating part of their operations to other countries implied Singapore could be losing its competitiveness.
The March data showed this was not the case as exports of data processing machines, which included disk-drives, rose by 3.8 percent after contracting 11.3 percent in February, Liew said.

The Trade Development Board said the March decline in non-oil exports was largely due to continuing problems in certain pockets of the electronics industry, which accounts for around half Singapore's manufacturing output and close to 60 percent of its non-oil exports.

"Though it was less severe than the 7.9 percent contraction in the previous month, it reflected continued weakness in the global demand for some electronics and related products such as semiconductors," the board said.
Economists also said the better-than-expected trade figures eclipsed the sharp decline of 17.6 percent year-on-year in February retail sales announced on Sunday.
Traditionally, external demand accounts for about 70-80 percent of total demand in the Singapore economy while retail sales measure domestic demand, they said.
Liew said he did not expect retail sales to shrink much more from current levels.
"I think the decline is seasonal," he said. "There may have been some people tightening their belts because of the slowdown in the economy." US$1 = S$1.44
